summary: This informational document analyzes threats against Internet mail that signature-based mail authentication, especially DomainKeys Identified Mail, is meant to address. It discusses who the bad actors are, where they are, what they can do and what they hope to achieve.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4686 examines how attackers can misuse email identities and signature systems. It explains what a verified DKIM signature establishes and which threats need other safeguards.

questions: what does a dkim signature prove
subtitle: The threats that signature-based email authentication was designed to address

tldr.problem: Email can claim an origin that did not send it, and attackers can also misuse valid signing systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4686 analyzes attacker capabilities, locations, goals, and attacks against message signatures and signing-practice records.
tldr.outcome: This Informational threat analysis guides DKIM design. It also explains that a valid signature identifies a signing domain, not a trustworthy person or message.

facts.label: DKIM verifies
facts.value: Message content and selected headers, not SMTP envelope fields

today: RFC 4686 is an Informational threat analysis, not an Internet Standard. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Threat Model
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a domain attach a cryptographic signature to an email. A recipient can retrieve the domain's public key and check that someone with the matching private key attested to the signed message content.

RFC 4686 analyzes threats to signature-based mail authentication. It distinguishes the message content from SMTP envelope details, which DKIM does not verify, and considers attackers inside and outside the sender's and recipient's administrative units.
sections.plainLanguage: A DKIM signature can show that a domain's key approved parts of an email. It does not verify the SMTP envelope or prove that the person or message is trustworthy.

sections.title: Attackers and Their Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC considers attackers with different resources and motives, from senders of unwanted mail to financially motivated attackers who may target Internet infrastructure. Some use compromised computers, registered domains, or large collections of harvested messages.

Depending on their resources, attackers may forge headers, send unsigned messages, replay signed messages, submit mail through several systems, or attack DNS and routing. The analysis also considers insiders and malware within the sender's or recipient's administrative unit.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may send forged mail, replay a signed message, or target the systems that publish keys. Some threats come from inside an email provider's own network.

sections.title: Misuse of Identities and Signatures
sections.content:
Attackers may claim arbitrary identities or impersonate a particular sender to exploit trust, commit fraud, or damage a domain's reputation. The RFC calls a reputation attack that sends unwanted mail in another party's name a 'joe-job'. Similar-looking domain names can also mislead recipients.

Other attacks target the signing system itself. Examples include theft of signing keys, replay of signed messages, denial of service against verifiers or key services, misuse of partial-body signatures, and attempts to exploit weaknesses in signature algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can imitate a sender, misuse a domain that the attacker controls, or resend an old signed message. Attackers may also target the keys and services used to check signatures.

sections.title: Limits and Design Requirements
sections.content:
A valid DKIM signature shows that a signing domain attested to message content; it does not show that the signer is benign. DKIM is not directly effective against malicious users or compromised systems inside the sender's administrative unit before signing, or against threats inside the recipient's unit.

The RFC says signing practices that declare a domain signs all its messages can help verifiers treat unsigned mail differently. It also derives design requirements: key and signing-practice records should be cacheable and available from geographically separated servers, and signature algorithms should be identified in key records.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature does not prove that an email is safe or that its author is honest. Other safeguards are needed for compromised systems, misleading names, and attacks inside a sender's or recipient's network.
